turns.output: Every family has a dish that tells its story, and in ours, that dish is chicken adobo. Passed down from my grandmother to my mother and now to me, this recipe carries the warmth of countless Sunday dinners and the comfort of a kitchen filled with familiar aromas. The tangy bite of vinegar, the savory depth of soy sauce, and the gentle sweetness of garlic and bay leaves come together in a sauce so rich you'll want to spoon it over every grain of rice on your plate. What makes this version special is the patience behind it: we let the chicken simmer slowly until the meat is tender and the flavors have melted together. It's a dish that asks for little but gives back a great deal, and I'm thrilled to share it with you.

Every Filipino family has a version of chicken adobo, and ours has been passed down through three generations of kitchens. My grandmother never measured anything. She would pour soy sauce and vinegar into a heavy clay pot, toss in garlic cracked open with the flat of a knife, and let the chicken simmer until the sauce turned dark, glossy, and sharp with tang. When I was young, I thought adobo was simply dinner. Now I understand it is a story about patience, memory, and making something nourishing from humble ingredients. This recipe captures her method as closely as I can translate it. It is forgiving, deeply savory, and perfect served over a mound of steamed white rice. I hope it brings your family to the table as often as it brought mine.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. When that sunlight travels through our atmosphere, which is the layer of air surrounding Earth, it bumps into tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the wavelengths of light, and this causes something called scattering, which means the light gets bounced around in all directions.

Different colors of light have different wavelengths. Blue and violet light have short, small wavelengths, so they scatter much more strongly than red and orange light, which have long wavelengths. Violet light scatters even more than blue, but there are a few reasons we see the sky as blue instead of violet. The sun emits less violet light than blue, some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

So when you look up on a clear day, you're seeing blue light that has been scattered down to your eyes from all across the sky. When you look toward the sun, you see the remaining light, which looks yellowish-white because much of the blue has been scattered away.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere to reach you, so most of the blue scatters out and you see reds and oranges instead.

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue? The answer has to do with sunlight and the air around us.

Sunlight may look white, but it is actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. When sunlight enters our atmosphere, the layer of air that wraps around Earth, it bumps into tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the waves of light passing through them.

Here is the key idea: shorter light waves, like blue and violet, get scattered in many directions much more strongly than longer waves, like red and orange. Scientists call this Rayleigh scattering, after the physicist Lord Rayleigh.

As sunlight bounces around the sky, blue light reaches your eyes from every direction. Red and orange light mostly keep traveling in a straight line. That is also why sunsets look red: at evening, sunlight passes through much more air to reach you, and most of the blue has been scattered away.

You might ask why the sky isn't violet, since violet scatters even more. The sun gives off less violet light, and our eyes respond better to blue, so blue is what we see.

Next time you look up on a clear day, remember that the blue you see is sunlight being scattered by the air all around you.

A browser cache is a storage space on your computer or phone where your web browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit, such as images, stylesheets, scripts, and sometimes entire pages.

Here's why it matters. Downloading files over the internet takes time. When you first visit a website, your browser fetches everything it needs and saves copies in the cache. The next time you visit that site, or move to another page that uses the same files (like a logo that appears on every page), the browser can load those items from your local storage instead of downloading them again. This makes pages load faster and saves data.

The cache follows rules set by the website. A site can tell your browser how long a file stays valid, for example "keep this image for one week." After that time, the browser checks with the server to see whether the file has changed. If it has, the browser downloads the new version; if not, it keeps using the cached copy.

You can usually see your cache's contents in your browser's settings or developer tools. Clearing it can fix problems, such as a page not showing recent changes, because the browser will then download fresh copies. The trade-off is that the next visit may be slightly slower.

In short, the browser cache is a local memory of website files that speeds up browsing and reduces unnecessary downloads.

A browser cache is a storage space on your computer or phone where your web browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit. These files can include images, logos, style sheets, scripts, and even entire web pages.

Here is why it matters. Normally, when you open a website, your browser has to download every file that makes up the page. That takes time and uses data. The cache offers a shortcut. The first time you visit a site, the browser saves copies of its files in the cache. The next time you visit, it checks the cache first. If the files are still there and haven't changed, it loads them from your device instead of downloading them again.

The result is faster loading, less data use, and a smoother experience, especially on slow connections.

Websites control how long files stay in the cache. A site might tell your browser to keep a logo for a week but to check the news headlines every few minutes. When a file expires, the browser asks the website whether it has changed. If it has, the browser downloads the new version.

You can clear your cache at any time through your browser's settings. This can fix problems like pages that look outdated or broken, though it means sites will load a bit slower the next time you visit them.

One year ago, I became an engineering manager. I thought the hardest part would be the technical decisions. It wasn't.

Here's what I actually learned:

- **Your output now is your team's output.** I used to measure success by what I shipped. Now it's by what my team ships, and that means getting out of the way more than I'd like.
- **One-on-ones aren't optional.** Skipping them to "save time" cost me more trust than any project delay ever did.
- **Say "I don't know" out loud.** My team trusts me more now that I admit gaps instead of faking certainty.
- **Protect your engineers from chaos.** Absorbing shifting priorities so they can focus has been the most valuable thing I do each week.

I'm still figuring this out every day. If you're new to management, what's one lesson you wish someone had told you earlier?

#EngineeringManagement #Leadership #SoftwareEngineering

One year ago, I became an engineering manager. Here's what I wish someone had told me on day one.

My best engineering skills didn't transfer automatically. Writing code was my comfort zone, and I had to learn that my job now is to multiply the team's output, not to be the fastest coder in the room.

Calendar time is the real currency. I went from having long stretches to focus to living in back-to-back meetings. Protecting my team's focus time became one of the most important things I do each week.

One-on-ones matter more than status updates. The most useful conversations weren't about tickets. They were about career goals, frustrations, and what people needed to do their best work.

Finally, admitting "I don't know, let me find out" builds more trust than pretending to have every answer.

What's one lesson you learned in your first year leading people?

**Pride and Prejudice** by Jane Austen (1813)

The novel follows Elizabeth Bennet, the witty and independent second daughter of a country gentleman family in early nineteenth-century England. With five unmarried daughters and an entailed estate that will pass to a distant cousin, the Bennets face financial insecurity, making marriage a pressing concern. Elizabeth initially clashes with Fitzwilliam Darcy, a wealthy and aloof man whose slighting remarks at a local ball wound her pride. Her prejudice deepens when Darcy seems to separate her beloved sister Jane from Mr. Bingley, and when the charming Mr. Wickham tells her a damaging story about Darcy.

As the story unfolds, Elizabeth learns that her judgments have been hasty and that Wickham is not who he appears to be. Darcy, in turn, confronts his own arrogance and reconsiders his assumptions about Elizabeth's family and social standing. Through a series of misunderstandings, revelations, and acts of genuine character, the two gradually come to respect and love one another.

The novel explores themes of pride and prejudice, showing how first impressions and social rank can distort judgment. It also critiques the economic realities that drive marriage decisions, contrasting mercenary alliances with marriages founded on mutual esteem. Ultimately, Austen argues that self-knowledge, humility, and moral integrity matter more than wealth or status.

Jane Austen's *Pride and Prejudice* (1813) follows Elizabeth Bennet, the witty second daughter of a country family. Because their estate is entailed to a male cousin, the Bennet daughters must marry well to secure their futures, and their mother is determined to see them wed. When the wealthy Charles Bingley and his proud friend Fitzwilliam Darcy arrive in the neighborhood, the community buzzes with speculation. Darcy's snobbish remark at a local ball offends Elizabeth, and she grows more prejudiced against him after the charming officer George Wickham tells her a false story of Darcy's cruelty.

As the story unfolds, Elizabeth's first impressions are challenged. Darcy proposes, but his insulting pride prompts her sharp refusal. Later, a letter reveals Wickham's deceit and Darcy's honorable conduct, forcing Elizabeth to confront her own misjudgment. Darcy also quietly resolves a family scandal involving her younger sister Lydia, and the two eventually reconcile.

The novel explores the dangers of hasty judgment and the damage caused by excessive pride and vanity. Austen also satirizes the social pressures on women who depended on marriage for security. By contrasting marriages of convenience with those built on mutual respect and genuine affection, she argues that character matters more than wealth or status, and that self-knowledge is essential to happiness.

1/5 Clever code impresses the person who wrote it, for about a week. Simple code serves everyone who reads it afterward, and that's where the real value is. Code is read far more often than it's written.

2/5 Clever tricks save a few keystrokes but cost comprehension. A one-liner that packs three operations, a bitmask, and an implicit type coercion makes the next reader stop, squint, and slow down. Every pause is a tax paid by your whole team.

3/5 Debugging is where clever code really hurts. When something breaks at 2 a.m., you need the logic to be obvious. Boring, explicit code gives you a clear path from symptom to cause. Clever code makes you reverse-engineer the author's mind first.

4/5 Simple doesn't mean naive. It means the solution's complexity matches the problem's complexity, no more. Use plain loops, descriptive names, and small functions. Save the advanced techniques for when they're truly needed, and comment them when you do.

5/5 Ask yourself: "Could a tired teammate understand this in 30 seconds?" If not, rewrite it. The goal isn't to show how smart you are. It's to make the next change safe, fast, and boring. Boring code ships.

1/5
Clever code feels good to write. Simple code is what you'll be grateful for at 2am when production is down. Here's why simple beats clever.

2/5
Code is read far more often than it's written. The author spends an hour on a tricky one-liner, and every future reader spends ten minutes decoding it. Optimize for the reader, not the writer's ego.

3/5
Clever code hides its assumptions. A dense bit trick or a chain of nested ternaries works until someone changes one thing, and then nobody can tell what it was supposed to do.

4/5
Debugging takes twice as much effort as writing the code. If you used all your cleverness to build it, you have none left to fix it. Boring code is easier to trace, test, and hand off.

5/5
Aim for code that a tired junior engineer could understand on their first day. Clear names, small functions, obvious control flow. Save the cleverness for the problem, not the implementation.
